clue.text: Producer of stage lighting for Pyramus and Thisbe

definitions.text: Producer of stage lighting for Pyramus and Thisbe

parts.words: Producer of stage lighting for Pyramus and Thisbe
parts.note: in A Midsummer Night's Dream the mechanicals' play of Pyramus and Thisbe has a character carrying a lantern to stand for moonshine

explanation.surface: A question about who rigged the lights for an amateur production of Pyramus and Thisbe.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's play, Starveling plays the figure in the moon, presenting moonshine with lantern, thorn bush and dog.
explanation.definitionFit: The character who 'presents moonshine' is literally the one lighting the mechanicals' stage.

clue.text: A short distance 'in light aircraft — prototype Jumbo

indicators.note: in says the next pieces are placed inside the aircraft's name

parts.note: the de Havilland Moth was a famous light aircraft
MM is a millimetre, a very short distance

explanation.surface: A tiny measurement inside a small plane leads to a giant jet's forerunner.
explanation.walkthrough: Jumbo is the name of a famous elephant (and jet); the extinct woolly elephant is its forerunner.
explanation.definitionFit: The extinct woolly elephant is an ancestor of today's big jumbos, the elephants.

clue.text: No neo-Edwardian was so famous

parts.note: a Teddy boy, or Ted, was a 1950s youth in neo-Edwardian dress

explanation.surface: A claim that no Teddy boy ever became a celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: Teddy boys were British youths of the 1950s who wore revived Edwardian fashions: drape jackets and drainpipe trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone well known and celebrated is remarked upon by many.

clue.text: The age in which Kipling wrote

definitions.text: The age in which Kipling wrote

parts.words: The age in which Kipling wrote
parts.note: seems to ask for Kipling's era, but points to the title of his poem 'In the ... Age', about a Stone Age bard

explanation.surface: A question about the historical period when Kipling was writing.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling actually wrote in the Victorian era; the clue means his poem's title, in which the speaker sang in the New Stone Age.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's poem title names the New Stone Age, the period the speaker says he wrote in.

clue.text: The appearance, it's said, of one who may succeed

indicators.note: it's said marks a word heard aloud but spelt otherwise

parts.note: an air is a manner or appearance, as in 'an air of confidence'

explanation.surface: Talk of how a likely successor looks, as people say.
explanation.definitionFit: The next in line inherits a title or estate when its holder dies.

clue.text: Played majestically in Hollywood the West's also taking in the South

parts.note: Mae West was a Hollywood star, so the West's is MAE'S

indicators.note: taking in means one word holds another inside it

parts.note: too means also
S is the abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: Mae West's Hollywood performance, also including the South, was played in grand style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the West' is not a region but Mae West, the Hollywood actress.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical direction meaning in a stately, dignified manner.

clue.text: Bid perhaps for grappling iron

indicators.note: grappling suggests letters wrestled together and jumbled

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: A bid made for a grappling hook at an auction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grappling' mixes FOR with FE, the symbol for iron.
explanation.definitionFit: A bid at auction is one kind of proposal to buy.

clue.text: Salad's just what the old king

parts.note: Old King Cole of the nursery rhyme, so the old king's is COLE'S
the law is what is just

explanation.surface: Salad is exactly what the old king ordered.
explanation.walkthrough: Old King Cole is the 'merry old soul' of the nursery rhyme; his word would be law.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabbage salad dressed with mayonnaise is a familiar side dish.

clue.text: Matchless poetess involved in 11

indicators.note: involved means twisted up, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: the answer to 11 across

explanation.surface: A peerless poetess was involved in clue 11.
explanation.walkthrough: Katherine Philips, a 17th-century poet, was known as 'the Matchless Orinda'.
explanation.definitionFit: Pen name of the poet Katherine Philips, whose admirers called her matchless.

clue.text: High-flier having ended a brilliant career

definitions.text: High-flier having ended a brilliant career

parts.words: High-flier having ended a brilliant career
parts.note: read as a successful person who has retired, but literally a shooting star whose fiery path through the sky is over and which has landed

explanation.surface: A tribute to a high achiever whose glittering career has come to an end.
explanation.definitionFit: A shooting star that survives its blazing flight and lands is a stone fallen from space.

clue.text: Stump from which some orators may speak

definitions.meaning: to stump someone is to baffle them, as a hard question does

definitions.text: from which some orators may speak
definitions.meaning: debaters in a chamber speak from the open area of the house, holding it while they talk

explanation.definitionFit: To baffle is also to floor someone; and a speaker who 'has the floor' addresses the assembly.

clue.text: Appoint as minister, or Hamlet as prince, say?

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: say signals that a word spoken aloud gives the letters

parts.note: Hamlet is the Prince of Denmark, so a Dane

explanation.surface: A puzzle about appointing a clergyman, or casting Hamlet as a prince.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' tells you DANE is heard, not spelt: write it DAIN to finish the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To make someone a minister of the church is to confer holy orders on them.

clue.text: Swimmer shows way to press forward

parts.note: ST is short for street, a way
to urge on is to press forward

explanation.surface: A competitor at the pool demonstrates a route to push ahead.
explanation.definitionFit: A large fish, the source of caviar, is a swimmer.

clue.text: Once called audibly the utmost degree

indicators.note: audibly means the word heard is spelt differently in the grid

parts.note: hight is an archaic word meaning named or called

explanation.surface: A phrase that was once named out loud as the very highest level.
explanation.walkthrough: HIGHT is an old poetic past participle, 'called', as in 'a knight hight Sir Roland'.
explanation.definitionFit: The peak or zenith of something, as in 'the height of fashion'.

clue.text: Muscovite in a one-goal result proves hostile

indicators.note: in puts the mineral inside the score

parts.note: a score of one-nil, written I NIL with I as one
muscovite is a common kind of the mineral mica

explanation.surface: A Russian in a one-nil game turns out unfriendly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Muscovite' looks like a Moscow native but is a mineral, a type of MICA.
explanation.definitionFit: Unfriendly or harmful, like an enemy.

clue.text: Basil was over her Lorenzo's head

definitions.text: Basil was over her Lorenzo's head

parts.words: Basil was over her Lorenzo's head
parts.note: in Keats's poem the heroine buries her murdered lover's head in a pot and plants the herb basil over it

explanation.surface: It looks like a man named Basil having power over a woman's lover.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats's poem is subtitled 'The Pot of Basil'; basil is the herb, not a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats's tragic heroine grew the herb in a pot holding her lover Lorenzo's severed head.

clue.text: Hazardous game for the serpent of old Nile

definitions.text: Hazardous game for the serpent of old Nile

parts.words: Hazardous game for the serpent of old Nile
parts.note: Cleopatra, called the serpent of old Nile; the cue game has scoring shots called hazards

explanation.surface: A dangerous pastime played by a snake from the Nile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hazardous' is not risky: a hazard is a scoring stroke in this cue game. Shakespeare gives it to Cleopatra anachronistically.
explanation.definitionFit: A cue sport with hazards that Shakespeare's Cleopatra proposes to play.

clue.text: Where fools are blissfully ignorant and the birds are gorgeous

definitions.meaning: a fool's version of heaven is a state of happy delusion
a family of brilliantly plumed New Guinea birds is named after heaven

explanation.definitionFit: A fool's heaven is a state of happy delusion; the brilliantly plumed birds are birds of heaven.

clue.text: Bird — that which is seen round Scotland's isle

indicators.note: round says one word is placed around another, enclosing it

parts.note: what can mean that which, as in 'do what you like'
inch is a Scottish word for a small island

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher describes the bird that can be spotted around a Scottish island.
explanation.definitionFit: A small brown songbird of open country, related to the stonechat.

clue.text: Street Browning visited going round in this headgear?

indicators.note: going means a letter goes missing from the word

parts.note: Elizabeth Barrett lived at Wimpole Street, where Robert Browning courted her
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A street Browning used to visit, with a nun in a head covering passing by.
explanation.walkthrough: Wimpole Street, in London, is famous from 'The Barretts of Wimpole Street'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cloth covering the head and neck, worn by medieval women and some nuns.

clue.text: Wind instrument for communication commonly

definitions.meaning: a device that produces a current of air, like a fan or bellows
in British slang a telephone, the means of talking to someone

explanation.definitionFit: A fan or bellows is a device for blowing air; in British slang the telephone is also called this.

clue.text: Titian beauty number one in the Kremlin?

definitions.meaning: Titian red is an auburn hair colour named after the painter's models
the leader of the communists, the Reds

explanation.definitionFit: A woman with auburn hair; also, jokingly, the chief of the communist Reds.

clue.text: Ironclad might one surmise? Not this vessel

definitions.text: Ironclad might one surmise? Not this vessel

parts.words: Ironclad might one surmise? Not this vessel
parts.note: the first word of the name suggests armour, chain mail, but the ship actually carries letters

explanation.surface: A warning that a ship's name might wrongly suggest it is armour-plated.
explanation.walkthrough: MAIL is armour as well as post, so the name seems to mean an armoured ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship carrying the post, not a vessel clad in chain mail.

clue.text: Buddhist priest put together black continental cricket team

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
onze is French for eleven, a team of cricketers

explanation.surface: A Buddhist priest assembles a black team of cricketers from the Continent.
explanation.walkthrough: A cricket team is an eleven; 'continental' asks for the French word.
explanation.definitionFit: A Buddhist monk of China or Japan.

clue.text: Man, say, taken in by doctor is caused to go wrong

indicators.note: taken in by says the first item sits inside the next one

parts.note: MD is Doctor of Medicine
the Isle of Man is an example of an isle

explanation.surface: A man is admitted by his doctor and is sent off course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' looks like a person, but with 'say' it is the Isle of Man, an example of an ISLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone led astray or deceived has been steered into error.

clue.text: A jungle climber's name inter alia perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints the letters may be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: A jungle climber's name, among other things, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges N with ALIA; 'inter' puts the N among them.
explanation.definitionFit: A woody vine that climbs up trees in tropical forests.

clue.text: Run fast or hide

definitions.meaning: to hurry along at speed, as rain does
an animal's skin with the fur on

explanation.definitionFit: To dash along at speed; also an animal's skin with its fur.

clue.text: Find out what's in the clear, naturally

indicators.note: what's in says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Discover what is plainly visible in clear, natural terms.
explanation.definitionFit: To discover a fact is to come to know it.

clue.text: Putting a beer in it craftily could make him drunk

indicators.note: craftily suggests letters cunningly rearranged into a new word

explanation.surface: Slipping beer into someone's drink on the sly would get him intoxicated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'craftily' rearranges the nine letters of 'a beer in it'.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as a noun, the word means a habitual drunkard.

clue.text: But as its monarch Alexander went unrecorded

definitions.text: But as its monarch Alexander went unrecorded

parts.words: But as its monarch Alexander went unrecorded
parts.note: Alexander Selkirk, the castaway, was 'monarch of all I survey' on his island, yet had no radio record choices, unlike guests on a famous BBC programme

explanation.surface: A remark that a monarch called Alexander left no record of his reign.
explanation.walkthrough: Desert Island Discs is a long-running BBC radio show in which guests choose records to take to an imaginary island; Selkirk, the real castaway in Cowper's poem, had none.
explanation.definitionFit: Selkirk ruled over an uninhabited isle alone, with no records to play there.
